title: Why Jailbreaks Succeed in Diffusion Language Models: An Energy Landscape Analysis
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 25 Sep 2026]
    Title:Why Jailbreaks Succeed in Diffusion Language Models: An Energy Landscape Analysis
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Existing attacks and defenses for diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) target specific vulnerabilities but lack a shared framework explaining why attacks succeed. We propose one by interpreting safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape: a well-aligned model routes harmful queries toward safe outputs through an energy barrier that separates the two regions. Current jailbreak attacks reduce to two strategies for circumventing this barrier: obscuring the query's safety disposition at initialisation, or intervening mid-trajectory to force the denoising path across the energy barrier. From this perspective and the result that masked diffusion models minimise kinetic energy during denoising, we derive three complementary, training-free detection signals: a step-0 ratio that reads the initial safety disposition from the logit distribution before generation begins, and two trajectory-velocity signals that track kinetic energy in complementary subspaces of the logit space. An attack must either reveal its intent at initialisation or expend kinetic energy to cross the barrier in at least one monitored subspace, so the three signals cover each other's blind spots in the energy budget by construction. Evaluation across three dense dLLMs (LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-7B) and a sparse mixture-of-experts dLLM (LLaDA-MoE-7B) confirms this complementarity. In stress tests of known attacks, every configuration that evades detection also fails to produce harmful content, suggesting that the detection and barrier-crossing thresholds are hard to separate.

report.summary: A new energy-landscape framework explains diffusion LLM jailbreaks and derives three training-free detection signals that catch attacks by monitoring initial safety disposition and denoising trajectory energy.
report.background: Diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising a masked or noisy sequence, unlike autoregressive LLMs. Safety alignment in these models has been studied mainly through ad hoc attacks and defenses, with no shared explanation for why jailbreaks work. This paper proposes interpreting alignment as shaping a denoising energy landscape: safe and harmful outputs occupy separate regions separated by an energy barrier. Jailbreaks either obscure a query's safety disposition at initialisation or intervene mid-trajectory to force the denoising path across that barrier. Because masked diffusion minimises kinetic energy during denoising, the authors derive training-free detectors and test them on LLaDA and Dream models, including a sparse mixture-of-experts variant.
key_points: The paper frames safety alignment as an energy barrier between safe and harmful output regions. A jailbreak must either hide the query's unsafe intent at initialisation or inject enough kinetic energy during denoising to cross the barrier. This turns many known attack tactics into two high-level strategies and gives defenders a unified target.

From this view come three training-free detection signals. A step-0 ratio reads the initial logit distribution before generation starts. Two trajectory-velocity signals track kinetic energy in complementary subspaces of logit space. Since an attack must reveal intent early or spend energy in at least one monitored subspace, the signals cover each other's blind spots by construction.

The authors evaluate the detectors on three dense diffusion LLMs—LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, and Dream-7B—plus a sparse mixture-of-experts model, LLaDA-MoE-7B. Results confirm the complementarity of the three signals across architectures. The approach is training-free, so it can be added at inference time without modifying model weights.

Stress tests with known attacks show a striking result: every configuration that evades detection also fails to produce harmful content. This suggests detection and barrier-crossing thresholds are hard to separate. In other words, if an attack stays below the detector's radar, it likely lacks the energy needed to actually jailbreak the model.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the work offers a principled, diffusion-specific safety framework and lightweight runtime monitors that need no retraining. Developers can instrument denoising steps to compute step-0 ratios and trajectory velocities, potentially catching jailbreaks before harmful content emerges. It also highlights that safety evaluation for dLLMs cannot simply copy autoregressive benchmarks; attack surfaces involve initialisation and denoising trajectories. For regular users, this may mean safer diffusion-based assistants and fewer successful jailbreaks, but also possible extra latency, refusals, or telemetry. The tight coupling between detectability and harmfulness suggests robust safety may be achievable, though it remains an arms race as attackers adapt.
report.tools: Follow the LLaDA family (LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, LLaDA-MoE-7B) and Dream-7B on Hugging Face to reproduce dLLM behaviour. Watch the paper's arXiv/alphaXiv page for official code. Useful companions include Hugging Face Transformers for inference hooks, JailbreakBench and HarmBench for adapted safety tests, and open masked-diffusion training code such as LLaDA or DiffuLLaMA. A small detector library could expose step-0 logit ratios and per-step kinetic-energy monitors.
